title: Water for the Other Side
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The spreadsheet said we had enough water.

The people waiting at the east end of the bridge said otherwise.

I stared at the figures and felt my face grow warm. The table I'd made showed thirty containers delivered to Riverstone Terrace, twelve to the clinic, eight to Brasswatch Yard, and six to the temporary shelter on the ridge. The total matched the supply account.

It was beautiful arithmetic.

It was a terrible distribution.

Katara stood beside me, reading the paper.

"How many people are at the east shelter?" she asked.

"Eighteen."

"And at the west?"

"Seven."

"How many containers?"

"Six east. Ten west."

She tapped the page.

"There's our problem."

The bridge had remained closed while the supports were repaired and tested after the storm. People could use the longer ridge route, but not every family could carry heavy containers that distance. The supply team had delivered water to the places closest to the storage depot first, then sent what remained to the harder-to-reach shelter.

Nobody had set out to be cruel.

The process had been convenient for the people carrying the crates, not fair to those who needed them.

I reached for my pencil.

"We can fix the numbers."

"Eventually," Katara said. "But first we need to talk to the people who are short."

We walked to the east shelter with Aang. The wind was still strong along the canal, and the lower path smelled of wet stone. A temporary ramp led into the hall, built after Edda's access inspection.

A woman named Sela greeted us at the door.

"Do you have water?"

"Some," Katara said. "Not enough yet. We're checking what everyone needs."

Sela pointed to a row of empty vessels.

"Some of us can drink from the spring if we carry it. Others can't carry the distance. The oldest person here needs water brought to her, and the family with the baby is boiling what they can find."

Katara nodded.

"Then they go first."

I wrote down the specific needs without putting private names on the public board.

Aang looked at the route.

"I could carry water across the canal with bending."

Sela looked at him.

"You could. What happens when you leave?"

He hesitated.

"We need a system that doesn't depend on me."

"Yes."

I felt a small rush of admiration. He'd learned to hear that question without treating it as an insult.

We returned to the square and called the distribution volunteers together. Mara had been packing supplies, Danse had helped design the carrying frames, and Greg had offered a morning shift with the handcart. Toph stood near the wall, listening to the movement through the stone floor.

I put the numbers on the board.

"These are the deliveries," I said. "But this is not the same as the needs."

One volunteer frowned.

"We delivered to every district."

"Yes. We didn't deliver proportionately to the people who couldn't access the other supplies."

Another looked embarrassed.

"We used the closest route first."

"I know. That's why we're changing it."

Toph tapped the floor.

"Your chart counts containers. It doesn't count the distance a person has to drag them."

I looked at her.

"Exactly."

We made a new plan with actual requirements. Katara confirmed the clinic's medical supply needs. Sela arranged a contact person at the east shelter without making the residents' private details public. Danse checked the handcart load. Edda tested the route so the deliveries wouldn't block the accessible path.

Aang offered to carry the heaviest containers for the first round, with two local volunteers learning the handling process for later shifts.

No one was assigned more than they'd agreed to do.

The revised plan meant the west shelter would receive fewer extra containers for one day. Some residents complained. They had been relieved to have a reserve and did not like hearing that it had been allocated unevenly.

I couldn't blame them for feeling anxious.

I could still tell the truth.

"We're not taking away your minimum needs," I explained. "We're correcting a distribution that left another group without theirs."

A man near the depot folded his arms.

"Easy for you to say."

He was right about one thing: I was not the person who would have to walk farther for water if the plan failed.

"Then help us test it," I said.

He looked surprised.

"We need your experience of the route. And if you find a problem, I want to know."

He did.

The second delivery went better. The east shelter received its immediate supplies before evening. The west retained enough for confirmed needs. The public ledger showed the changes and the reasons, without turning vulnerable households into a list of people to be judged.

We returned home exhausted.

Katara washed the dust from her hands and looked at my spreadsheet, now covered in corrections.

"Do you still like it?" she asked.

"Not particularly."

She smiled.

"Good. That means it's being used."

Toph sat at the table with a bowl of soup.

"Spreadsheets are like people," she announced. "They get annoying when they think they're always right."

Aang laughed.

I sat beside her.

"Are you comparing me to a spreadsheet?"

"Only on your worst days."

Katara came around the table and rested a hand on my shoulder.

"You noticed a problem," she said. "Then you listened. That's what matters."

I looked at her.

"We still missed it for two days."

"Yes."

She didn't soften the truth.

Then she kissed my forehead.

"We'll do better tomorrow."

Later, when the dishes were done, Aang showed me the new route he'd drawn. It included shaded rest points, safe crossing times, and notes from the people who used the path daily. His handwriting was crooked from trying to fit too much information onto one page.

I smiled.

"It looks terrible."

"It works."

"That might be the new standard."

He grinned and leaned close.

"Then perhaps I can ask for something that doesn't fit in a table."

"What?"

"A quiet walk with you."

I took his hand.

We went outside beneath the lanterns.

The bridge remained closed. The water was still moving. The arithmetic was still imperfect.

But the people on the other side had water, and we'd stopped confusing a balanced column with a fair day.
